Methods how we work

Process writing

A text improves when it is rewritten. Most tasks go through three steps:

Draftwrite it fast Peer reviewa classmate checks Redraftmake it better

Four more methods

  • Peer review: you read and comment on a classmate’s text.
  • Case study: you solve a real problem with a text.
  • Portfolio: you collect your best drafts and redrafts.
  • Projects: you plan and write something bigger with a team.

Twelve words you will hear in this course again and again. Read the cards. Say each word aloud and make a sentence about yourself with a partner.

draftNOUN / VERB an early version of a text that you will improveMy first draft was too long.
redraftVERB write a text again to improve itredraft the conclusion
feedbackNOUN comments on your work that help you improveuseful feedback on my essay
peer reviewNOUN students reading and commenting on each other’s workpeer review in pairs
portfolioNOUN a collection of your work that shows progressadd a text to my portfolio
deadlineNOUN the time by which work must be finishedThe deadline is Friday.
assignmentNOUN a piece of work that a teacher setsa writing assignment
fluencyNOUN the ability to write easily, without long pausesFluency comes with practice.
accuracyNOUN the ability to write correctly, with few mistakesaccuracy in grammar
habitNOUN something you do regularly, often without thinkinga daily reading habit
make progressPHRASE improve gradually over timeShe is making fast progress.

Read like a detective

15 MIN

Before you read: a third-year student writes to new second-year students. What advice do you expect? Tick one.
work harder    work smarter    don’t worry at all

Letter to a Second-Year Writer

A student’s letter · about 400 words · B2 · written for this book (Kamola is fictional)

ADear second-year student, a year ago I sat in this room with the same book in my hands, and I felt nervous. I could speak English quite well, but writing was different. My sentences were too long, my ideas jumped around, and every red mark on my paper felt personal. Now I am in my third year, and I am writing to tell you what I wish someone had told me.

BFirst, good writers are not born; they are made. Our teacher repeats this every week, and now I believe it. Nobody writes a perfect text on the first try. Experienced writers write a draft, get feedback and then redraft. That is exactly what you are going to do in this course.

CSecond, reading feeds writing. I read something in English every day: a short article, a blog post, sometimes a chapter of a novel. I do not understand every word, and that is fine. I notice how writers start a paragraph, how they give examples and how they finish. Then I borrow their tools — but never their words!

DThird, small habits beat big plans. At the start of last year, I planned to write for two hours every Sunday. It never happened. Now I write for fifteen minutes every evening, usually in a notebook by my window. Some evenings I describe my day; on other evenings I try out a new linking word that I noticed in my reading. Fifteen minutes does not sound like much, but it adds up.

EFourth, feedback is a gift, not a punishment. During peer review, my partner Aziz often finds problems that I cannot see. At first I hated it. Now I ask for it, because two pairs of eyes see more than one. This month, we are reviewing each other’s course papers, and his comments are making my work much clearer.

FFinally, be patient with yourself. These days I am preparing for my exams, and I am still learning. I still make mistakes with articles, and I still rewrite my introductions three times. But I am not afraid of a blank page any more. I know what to do with it.

GSo open your notebook, set a small goal and start your journey. You will be surprised how far fifteen minutes a day can take you. Good luck — and enjoy the road!
Kamola, third-year student, Navoi

Kamola gives five tips. Number them in the margin as you read.
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs A–C, Group B on D–E, Group C on F–G. Read your part, agree on Kamola’s tip in it, then form mixed groups and teach it in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which of Kamola’s five tips is the most useful for you? Which one is the hardest to follow? Why?

Toolkit: present simple or continuous?

Writing about yourself? You need two tenses: one for habits, one for now and these days.

Find these sentences in the letter and complete them.

2. (C) I something in English every day.

3. (D) Now I for fifteen minutes every evening.

4. (A) Now I am in my third year, and I to tell you …

5. (E) This month, we each other’s course papers.

6. (F) These days I for my exams.

The rule card rule
TenseUse it for …Example from the letter
Present simple
I write · she writes		habits and routines (every day, usually, often)I read something in English every day.
facts and general truthsNobody writes a perfect first draft.
state verbs (know, believe, understand, want, need)I know what to do with it.
Present continuous
I am writing · we are writing		actions happening nowI am writing to tell you …
temporary situations and changes (these days, this month, this semester)His comments are making my work clearer.
  • he / she / it + -s: our teacher repeats ✓  ·  our teacher repeat ✗
  • am / is / are + -ing: we are reviewing ✓  ·  we reviewing ✗
  • State verbs stay simple: I understand ✓  ·  I am understanding ✗
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence

2. Dilnoza read English news every morning.
3. Look! The teacher write our deadline on the board.

Level up: write about yourself at C1

CONTINUED

A B2 writer says I am good at speaking, but writing is hard. A C1 writer says the same thing with more precision: the exact skill, how often, how sure — and what is changing.

ToolPhrasesExample
Precise topic sentence
vague → exact		is good at → has always been my strongest skill · is hard → remains a challengeWriting is hard for me. → Writing remains my greatest challenge.
Nominalisation
verb / adjective → noun		improve → improvement · confident → confidence · fluent → fluencyI improved a lot. → My improvement this year surprised me.
Hedging about yourself
honest, not absolute		I tend to … · I find it hard to … · on the wholeI tend to write very long sentences.
Stance adverbs
your attitude in one word		admittedly · gradually · increasingly · surprisinglyAdmittedly, my grammar is not perfect, but it is gradually improving.

☆Make it C1 rewrite

Rewrite each sentence with the word(s) in brackets. Keep the meaning.

B2 sentenceC1 sentence
1. I usually write very long sentences. (tend to)
2. I improved a lot this year. (improvement)
3. Writing is hard for me. (I find it)
4. My grammar is not perfect. (Admittedly)
5. I am good at speaking. (strongest skill)

Do not over-hedge

✗ I think maybe I perhaps tend to sometimes make some small mistakes.
✓ I tend to make mistakes with articles.  — one hedge per claim is enough, and a precise detail is better than three soft words.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own paragraph.

CriterionA C1 paragraph …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear main idea from the door to the window
O · Organisationhas one door, shelves with a point + example each, and a window, and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: present simple for habits, present continuous for now

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students wrote the Level 2 paragraph (Me as a learner of English). Mark both.

Student A
I am student of second course, and as a learner of English I am strong in speaking but weak in writing. I am learning English since school, so I very like speaking with tourists in Bukhara. Writing, however, is difficult for me because I am do many mistakes with tenses and articles. For example, last week my essay had twelve red marks. In my opinion I think the answer is regular practice. That is why this semester I want to do progress.
Student B
Speaking has always been my strongest skill, but writing remains a challenge. I tend to build long, ambitious sentences in which my ideas lose their way, and articles are a constant source of small errors. This semester, however, I am trying a simpler approach: shorter sentences, one idea per paragraph and fifteen minutes of writing every evening. Admittedly, progress is slow, yet each redraft feels a little clearer than the last.

Fix it · six typical errors in Student A

1. I am student of second course →

2. I am learning English since school →

3. I very like speaking →

4. I am do many mistakes →

5. In my opinion I think →

6. I want to do progress →

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Word Bazaar

8 MIN

Twelve words for writing about animals. Read the cards. Then say each word aloud and make a sentence with a partner.

remarkableADJ unusual or impressive enough to be noticeda remarkable journey
speciesNOUN a group of animals or plants of the same kindone species, two species
habitatNOUN the natural environment where an animal livesa mountain habitat
adapt (to)VERB change over time to suit new conditionsadapt to the cold
surviveVERB continue to live in spite of dangersurvive a long winter
endureVERB bear hardship or extreme conditions for a long timeendure the desert heat
migrateVERB move to another region regularly, usually each seasonStorks migrate south.
predatorNOUN an animal that hunts and kills others for foodWolves are predators.
preyNOUN an animal that is hunted and eaten by anotherMountain goats are the snow leopard’s prey.
herdNOUN a large group of animals that live and feed togethera herd of camels
camouflageNOUN colours or patterns that help an animal hideperfect camouflage on rocks
endangeredADJ at serious risk of disappearing completelyan endangered species

Level up · C1 words: adaptation (a feature that helps a species survive in its habitat) · nocturnal (active at night) · resilient (able to recover from hard conditions) · biodiversity (the variety of life in one place)

Word families: adapt → adaptation → adaptable · survive → survival → survivor · migrate → migration → migratory · prey → predator → predatory

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: what does built to survive mean? Tick one.
made by people    a body that suits its home    kept in a zoo

Built to Survive

A magazine article · about 460 words · B2 · written for this book

AThere are animals that live in places where a human would not last a single day. They cross burning deserts, climb icy mountains and fly over whole continents. How do they do it? Over a very long time, each species has adapted to its own difficult home. Here are five remarkable examples.

BThe Bactrian camel is perfectly designed for life in the desert. Its two humps do not hold water, as many people think; they store fat. When there is no food, this fat gives the camel energy. It can go for days without drinking, and it can close its nostrils to keep out sand. No wonder merchants on the Silk Road trusted camels to carry their goods for centuries.

CThe snow leopard is a true master of the cold. It lives high in the mountains of Central Asia, including the Tien Shan. Its thick fur keeps it warm, and its wide paws work like snowshoes. Its long tail helps it to balance on rocks, and when it rests, it wraps the tail around its body like a scarf. Because people so rarely see it, it is often called “the ghost of the mountains”. Today there are not many snow leopards left. The IUCN Red List lists the species as Vulnerable, and in Uzbekistan it is in the national Red Book and protected by law.

DThe white stork is famous for its long journeys. Every autumn, storks fly south to spend the winter in warmer lands, and every spring many of them return to the same nests. They do not flap their wings all the way; instead, they glide on rising warm air and save energy. In the old cities of Uzbekistan, storks’ nests were once a familiar sight on domes and minarets.

EThe Central Asian tortoise survives by doing very little. In the steppe, there is fresh grass only in spring, so the tortoise is active for just a few months a year. It eats as much as it can, and then it stays underground through the hot summer and the cold winter. Its slow life may look boring, but it is a clever plan.

FThe honeybee is a small insect with a surprising talent: it can give directions. In every hive there are thousands of bees. When one of them finds good flowers, it returns to the hive and performs a special “dance”. The direction and length of the dance tell the other bees which way to fly and how far to go.

GWhat do these animals have in common? Each of them has a body or a habit that solves a difficult problem. There is one problem, however, that they cannot solve alone: the loss of their habitats. Learning about these animals is the first step towards protecting them.

Look at the first sentence of B–F. What do you notice?
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs B–C, Group B on D–E, Group C on F–G. Find the first sentence of each paragraph and one detail that supports it. Then form mixed groups and teach your animals in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which animal in the article is the most remarkable? Which detail convinced you? Why?

Language toolkit: there is / there are

10 MIN

English needs a subject in every sentence. When you say that something exists somewhere, the subject is there.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the article and complete them.

1. (A) animals that live in places where a human would not last a single day.

2. (B) When no food, this fat gives the camel energy.

3. (F) In every hive thousands of bees.

4. (G) one problem, however, that they cannot solve alone.

UseExample
there is + a / an + singularThere is a nest on the dome.
there is + uncountableThere is no water here.
there are + pluralThere are many storks.
Is there … ? / Are there any … ?Are there any wolves?
there was / there wereThere were nests on minarets.

Uzbek → English

Özbekistonda laylaklar köp.
✗ In Uzbekistan have many storks.
✗ In Uzbekistan is many storks.
✓ There are many storks in Uzbekistan.

Çölda suv yöq.
✗ In the desert is no water.
✓ There is no water in the desert.

The topic-sentence formula

TOPIC (what?) + CONTROLLING IDEA (what exactly about it?) = a topic sentence
The snow leopard | is a true master of the cold.  ·  There are three reasons why | camels were the trucks of the Silk Road.

Too wide, too narrow or just right? judge

4. There are many animals in the world.

5. There are three reasons why storks are welcome guests in our towns.

6. A honeybee is an insect.

Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence

2. There are a camel in the picture.
3. It is no water in the desert in summer.

Level up: precise doors and cohesion

CONTINUED

At C1 your door is precise: the reader knows exactly what the room will prove. Inside the room, every sentence points back to the one before it, so the reader never gets lost.

ToolPhrasesExample
Precise controlling idea
vague → exact		is interesting → is remarkably well adapted to · is good at → is a master ofThe camel is interesting. → The camel is remarkably well adapted to life in the desert.
Nominalisation
verb → noun		adapt → adaptation · survive → survival · lose → loss · migrate → migrationStorks migrate every year. → Their annual migration covers thousands of kilometres.
This / these + noun
points back, links two sentences		this adaptation · this technique · these features · such behaviourStorks glide on warm air. This technique saves a great deal of energy.
Hedging
makes a claim less absolute		tend to · may · is often called · in most casesTortoises tend to spend most of the year underground.
☆Notice find it

Find one example of each tool in the article. Write it and the paragraph letter.

1. precise idea: ( )

2. noun from lose: ( )

3. this + noun: ( )

4. a hedge: ( )

Rewrite each sentence with the word(s) in brackets. Keep the meaning.

B2 sentenceC1 sentence
1. The snow leopard is very interesting. (master)
2. Storks fly south. It is a long journey. (migration)
3. Camels close their nostrils. It keeps out sand. (This ability)
4. Animals lose habitats. It is the main danger. (loss)
5. Tortoises always stay underground. (tend to)

Remember from Stop 1: do not over-hedge

✗ The camel may perhaps possibly be quite well adapted to the desert in some ways.
✓ The camel is remarkably well adapted to the desert.  — hedge only when you are not sure; one hedge per claim is enough.

The Blueprint: build it like a room

10 MIN

A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea. The reader comes in through the door (the topic sentence), looks at every shelf (the supporting sentences) and leaves through the window (the concluding sentence).

Part of the roomPart of the paragraphWhat goes insideSentences
The doorTopic sentenceTopic + controlling idea: what the whole paragraph will prove1
The shelvesSupporting sentences2–3 shelves; each shelf = one point + an example or detail (For example … · This means …)4–6
The windowConcluding sentenceThe main idea in new words, sometimes with a final thought1
Compare it think
SentenceParagraph (today)Essay (Stop 7 and later)
Sizeone line or twoabout 100–150 words250–300 words
Main ideaone piece of informationone idea, in the topic sentenceone position, in the thesis
Buildingone brickone rooma hovli: a house with several rooms

Which task asks for ONE paragraph? Tick one.

In about 120 words, describe an animal that is well adapted to its habitat.
Write a 250-word essay on how to protect wildlife in Central Asia.
Write one sentence about your favourite animal.

One paragraph has one topic sentence. If your paragraph has two, split it into two paragraphs.

Common traps

✗ In this paragraph I will write about camels.
✓ The camel is perfectly designed for desert life.
✗ The snow leopard it lives in the mountains.
✓ The snow leopard lives in the mountains.
✗ Camel is a remarkable animal.
✓ The camel is / Camels are remarkable animals.
✗ Camels can live without water many days.
✓ Camels can live without water for many days.
✗ It is an endangered specie.
✓ It is an endangered species.
✗ The tortoise adapted for the hot summer.
✓ The tortoise has adapted to the hot summer.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own paragraph.

CriterionA C1 paragraph …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear main idea from the door to the window
O · Organisationhas one door, shelves with a point + example each, and a window, and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: there is / there are, a subject in every sentence

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students wrote the first half of a paragraph for the model task (… an animal that is important in your country). Mark both.

Student A
Camel is very very interesting animal, and it is perfectly designed for life in the desert. First, it can survive without water. In desert is no water for many days, but camel it can live. Second, camel have two hump, and they store fat for energy. Third, it is very strong, so it carry many things for the people. In my opinion I think the camel is the most useful animal of the desert.
Student B
Few animals are as well equipped for the harsh conditions of Central Asia as the Bactrian camel. Contrary to popular belief, its two humps store fat rather than water, and this reserve allows it to survive for long periods without food. Its ability to close its nostrils during sandstorms is a further adaptation to its habitat. It is therefore hardly surprising that Silk Road merchants trusted this animal with their goods for centuries.

Fix it · six errors in Student A

1. Camel is very very interesting animal. →

2. In desert is no water. →

3. … but camel it can live. →

4. Camel have two hump. →

5. … it carry many things for the people. →

6. In my opinion I think … →

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Four Seasons, One Country

A travel magazine feature · about 440 words · B2 · written for this book

AIn early spring, the Fergana Valley turns pink and white. Thousands of apricot trees come into blossom, and their sweet, gentle fragrance fills the warm air. Bees hum among the branches, while fresh green grass covers the soft brown fields. After the long grey winter, the whole valley seems to wake up and smile.

BLast April, I stayed with my grandparents in a village near Namangan. One evening, the radio warned that a late frost was coming. After dark, my grandmother, my uncle and their neighbours lit small fires between the apricot trees. All night long, they took turns watching the fires. Finally, at sunrise, the cold grey smoke lifted, and most of the blossom had survived. I will never forget that night.

CSummer in the city and summer in the mountains are two different worlds. In Tashkent, the afternoon sun is scorching, and many people stay indoors until the evening. In the Chatkal foothills, on the other hand, the air remains fresh and cool, and streams of melted snow run between the rocks. However, both places share one summer habit: when the heat goes down, families sit outside and drink green tea.

DHot summers also bring a serious problem: in many regions, water is becoming scarce. In dry years, rivers carry less water from the mountains, and farmers find it harder to water their fields. One solution is drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of plants and wastes much less. Another solution is to plant trees along roads and canals, because their shade keeps the soil cooler.

EAutumn is the season of the bazaar. Golden melons lie in tall piles, purple and green grapes shine in old wooden boxes, and the air smells of ripe pomegranates and freshly baked bread. Sellers call out to every passer-by. One of them hands you a slice of melon, so sweet and juicy that it drips down your fingers.

FIn January, I finally saw real snow in the mountains. We left Tashkent at dawn in a shared taxi. At first, the road was grey and wet, but after an hour everything turned white. When we arrived in Chimgan, children were sliding down the slopes on plastic sledges. By the evening, my cheeks were red, my boots were wet, and I was completely happy.

GIn my opinion, autumn is the best time to visit Uzbekistan. The scorching heat is over, but the days are still warm and sunny. Moreover, the bazaars are full of fruit, and the beautiful old blue domes of Samarkand look even brighter under the clear sky. Every season has its charm, but if you can travel only once, I believe you should come in October.

Seven paragraphs, five paragraph types. Note the type of each in the margin.
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs A–B, Group B on C–D, Group C on E–G. Decide which house each paragraph lives in and find two signal words. Then form mixed groups and teach your paragraphs in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which paragraph made you most want to travel? Which house does it live in? Paragraphs B and F live in the same house: what do they have in common?

Language toolkit: adjectives that paint

10 MIN

A descriptive paragraph lives on adjectives and the five senses. But in English, adjectives stand in a fixed order — like guests at a wedding table.

Notice find it

Find these phrases in the article and complete them.

1. (A) fresh grass

2. (A) the long winter

3. (B) the cold smoke

4. (E) old boxes

5. (G) the beautiful old domes

The order of the table rule
1 Opinion2 Size3 Age4 Shape5 Colour6 Origin7 Material+ NOUN
beautifuloldbluedomes
hugeblackironpot
smallroundRishtanbowl

Three rules

  • Two or three adjectives are enough. The table shows the order of all groups, but one noun never needs all of them: five adjectives in a row tire the reader.
  • Commas: two opinion adjectives → comma (sweet, gentle fragrance); different groups → no comma (huge black iron pot).
  • Uzbek is flexible, English is strict: katta eski uy / eski katta uy → only a big old house ✓
Order it practise

1. (wooden / small / old) a table

2. (silk / beautiful / Uzbek) a scarf

3. (yellow / delicious / round) a melon

4. (white / huge) mountains

Paint it, don’t name it senses
👁 golden · misty · sparkling👂 humming · crunchy · echoing👃 fragrant · smoky👅 juicy · sour✋ icy · rough · soft

Rewrite each sentence with details for two senses.

2. The bazaar is busy in autumn.

Rich noun phrases
descriptive house		snow-capped · sun-baked · tree-lined · the … of …high white mountains → the snow-capped peaks of the Chatkal range
Precise contrast
comparison house		whereas · while · unlike X, … · by contrastUnlike the city, the foothills remain cool in July.
Nominalised causes
problem–solution house		a shortage of · the scarcity of · leads to · results inThe scarcity of water leads to smaller harvests.
Stance adverbs
opinion house		arguably · undoubtedly · admittedlyAutumn is arguably the best season to visit Samarkand.

CONTINUED

Two houses on the same street. Same parts — door, shelves, window — but different jobs.

House 1 · Descriptive
DOORAt sunset, the Kyzylkum desert becomes a sea of colour. SHELVESThe pale yellow sand slowly turns orange, then deep red, and long purple shadows stretch behind every small dune. The hot afternoon wind drops, and the only sound is the soft whisper of sand moving over the dunes. As the sun disappears, the air grows cool, but the sand still feels warm under your hands. WINDOWFor a few minutes, the hard, empty desert looks gentle and almost magical.
House 4 · Comparison
DOORSpring and autumn in Uzbekistan are similar in some ways but very different in others. SHELVESBoth seasons have mild, pleasant weather, so they are ideal for travelling. However, spring is the season of beginnings: the orchards come into blossom, and the fields are fresh and green. Autumn, in contrast, is the season of rewards: the leaves turn gold, and farmers harvest grapes, melons and pomegranates. WINDOWIn short, spring makes promises, whereas autumn keeps them.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own paragraph.

CriterionA C1 paragraph …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear main idea from the door to the window
O · Organisationhas the door, shelves and window of the right house, and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: adjectives in the right order, two or three per noun

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students answered the same task: Describe a place in Uzbekistan in your favourite season. Help the reader see, hear and feel it. Mark both.

Student A
Samarkand is very beautiful city in autumn. In autumn is not hot and not cold, and the blue old domes of the Registan shine in the sun. There are many many fruits in bazaar: yellow melons, red pomegranates and sweet grapes, and the air smells of fresh bread. Last year I visited to Registan with my family. In my opinion I think everybody must go to Samarkand in October.
Student B
In late October, Samarkand glows under a soft, golden light. The scorching heat of summer has given way to crisp mornings, and the tiled domes of the Registan shimmer against a cloudless sky. In the narrow streets of the old town, the air is thick with the smoky scent of tandir bread, while sellers call out over piles of sun-ripened pomegranates. Even the evening breeze, cool on your face, seems to carry the sweetness of the season.

hospitalityNOUN friendly, generous treatment of guestsUzbek hospitality is famous.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the title. What is the article about? Tick one.
recipes    table customs    restaurants

More Than a Meal

A magazine article · about 440 words · B2 · written for this book

AIn Uzbekistan, a meal is rarely just food. The word dastarkhan means the cloth that is spread for a meal, but it also means everything on it — and everyone around it. Visitors notice this quickly: a simple cup of tea can turn into an hour of conversation. So what makes the Uzbek table so special?

BThe first answer is hospitality. In many families, a guest is a person of honour, even if he or she arrives without warning. First, the host spreads the dastarkhan. Then bread, sweets, dried fruit and nuts appear. After that, tea is served, and only later does the main dish arrive.

CBread, or non, has a special place in this ritual. It is usually round and is often baked in a clay oven called a tandir. Many families never put non upside down, and they try never to throw it away. For example, dry bread may be used in other dishes instead. For many people, bread is a symbol of life itself. Therefore, it is broken by hand and shared.

DTea has its own rules as well. The host often pours tea into a small bowl, a piyola, and back into the teapot two or three times so that it brews well. In addition, a guest’s piyola is usually filled only halfway. This is not a sign of meanness. On the contrary, it means that the host wants to serve the guest again and again — and keep them talking.

EPlov, however, is the king of the table. It is cooked in a large kazan with rice, carrots, onions and meat, and every region proudly claims its own version. At weddings and big celebrations, it is often prepared early in the morning for hundreds of guests. Fast-food restaurants have also become very popular in big cities in recent years. It is not surprising, therefore, that UNESCO has recognised palov culture as part of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

FSome dishes are cooked only once a year. Sumalak, a sweet brown paste made from sprouted wheat, is prepared for Navruz, the spring holiday. Traditionally, women lead the cooking, but often the whole mahalla joins in: neighbours take turns stirring the kazan all night, while they sing, talk and make wishes. Although the work is hard, nobody wants to miss it, because the real ingredient is time spent together.

GToday, life in Uzbekistan is changing fast, and many young people eat on the go. However, the dastarkhan has not disappeared. On holidays, at weddings and on ordinary weekends, families still gather around it. Perhaps that is the secret: a dastarkhan does not just feed the body; it holds a family together.

One sentence in this article breaks unity. Mark it as you read.
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs A–C, Group B on D–E, Group C on F–G. Read your part, agree on its main idea, then form new mixed groups and teach it in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which tradition from the article is still strong in your family? Which one has changed? Why?

Language toolkit: linking words

10 MIN

Linking words are the mortar of a paragraph. Each one has a job — and its own punctuation.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the article and complete them.

1. (B) , the host spreads the dastarkhan. bread, sweets, dried fruit and nuts appear.

2. (C) , dry bread may be used in other dishes instead.

3. (C) , it is broken by hand and shared.

4. (D) , a guest’s piyola is usually filled only halfway.

5. (E) Plov, , is the king of the table.

6. (F) the work is hard, nobody wants to miss it.

The mortar box rule
JobLinking wordsPunctuation pattern
additionand · also · In addition, · Moreover,Tea is served. In addition, sweets appear.
contrastbut · However, · Although …,Plov is heavy. However, it is tasty.
sequenceFirst, · Then · After that, · Finally,First, wash the rice. Then fry the onions.
resultso · Therefore, · As a result,We were hungry, so we ate.
examplefor example, · for instance, · such asdishes such as plov and sumalak

Three rules

  • Between two sentences: full stop before, comma after → Plov is tasty. However, it is heavy.
  • but / so join one sentence: comma before → It was late, but we drank tea.
  • Although needs no partner: Although it was late, we drank tea. ✓ (…, but we drank tea ✗)
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. Plov is delicious, however it is quite heavy.
2. Although they came late, but we were happy.
3. We were hungry therefore we ate a lot.
4. At first, wash the rice in cold water.
5. I like dishes such as, plov and manti.

The Blueprint: bricks and mortar

10 MIN

A good paragraph has unity: every sentence is about one main idea. It also has coherence: the sentences follow a logical order, and linking words show how they connect.

Part of the wallPart of the paragraphWhat it does
The whole wallthe paragraphtalks about one main idea (unity)
The top stonetopic sentencenames the topic + the controlling idea
The brickssupporting sentencesreasons, details, examples — in a logical order
The mortarlinking wordsshows how the sentences connect (5 jobs)
The bottom stoneconcluding sentencerepeats the main idea in new words
A brick from another wallan off-topic sentencebreaks unity → take it out
Compare it think
UnityCoherence
The questionIs every sentence about the main idea?Does every sentence follow logically?
The problema brick from another wallbricks in the wrong order, no mortar
The repairremove the sentencereorder + add linking words

Which problem does each wall have? Tick one for each.

WallUnity problemCoherence problem
1. A paragraph about tea suddenly talks about the price of coffee.
2. A plov recipe puts the rice in the kazan before the meat.
3. Six short sentences about Navruz, with no linking words at all.
4. A paragraph about sumalak ends with a sentence about the weather in London.
5. The example of a wedding plov comes before the topic sentence it supports.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own paragraph.

CriterionA C1 paragraph …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear main idea from the top stone to the bottom stone
O · Organisationhas a top stone, bricks in a logical order and a bottom stone, and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: linking words with the right punctuation (Although without but; However, after a full stop)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students answered the model task (a food tradition in your family). Mark both.

Student A
In my family we have very nice tradition, it is plov on Friday. My father cook plov in a big kazan in the yard, and my brother and I lay the dastarkhan. Plov is very delicious and all people like it. Also my brother likes football very much. Although plov is heavy, but we eat a lot. Moreover we drink green tea. Moreover we talk about the week. So this is our tradition.
Student B
In my family, Friday plov is far more than a meal; it is a weekly ritual that brings three generations together. Preparations begin early in the morning, when my father lights the fire under the kazan. Meanwhile, the younger children lay out the dastarkhan and put the bread in its place of honour. By the time the rice is ready, the whole family has gathered, and the conversation often lasts longer than the meal itself.

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: who invented the telephone?   Sure? yes   not really

Who Owns an Idea?

A magazine article · about 430 words · B2 · written for this book

AAsk a group of students who invented the telephone, and most of them will give one name: Alexander Graham Bell. Ask who invented the light bulb, and the answer will probably be Thomas Edison. These answers are not completely wrong, but they hide a more interesting story. Behind almost every famous invention, there is a crowd of people whose names we have forgotten.

BThe telephone is a good example. In the 1870s, several inventors in different countries were working on ways to send the human voice along a wire. Bell received the patent, but some historians argue that others reached similar ideas at about the same time. Similarly, many people had made electric lamps before Edison. His team’s real achievement, as historians often explain, was to make the bulb practical and long-lasting.

CIn fact, ideas rarely appear from nowhere. Scientists build on the work of people who came before them, and those people built on earlier work too. Students in Uzbekistan know a good example: the word algorithm comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, the scholar from Khorezm whose books on mathematics were later translated and studied in Europe. Every computer program today carries a small trace of his work.

DSo who should get the credit? Patent systems offer one answer. A patent gives an inventor the right to control an invention for a limited time. In exchange, the inventor must explain publicly how it works. Supporters claim that this system is fair: the inventor is rewarded, and everyone else can learn from the idea and improve it later.

EUniversities face a similar question on a smaller scale. In academic writing, ideas are a kind of property. If a student uses another person’s words or ideas without saying where they came from, this is called plagiarism. Many universities now use software that compares students’ work with books, articles and websites. Teachers point out, however, that software can only find copied words; it cannot find stolen ideas.

FUsing sources is not the problem. In fact, good academic writing is full of other people’s ideas. The difference is honesty. A writer can quote an author’s exact words in quotation marks, paraphrase an idea in completely new words, or summarise a long text in a few sentences. In each case, the writer shows the source.

GThe history of invention suggests a simple lesson. No idea is born alone, and nobody’s work is entirely their own. Giving credit is not a sign of weakness. It is a way of saying thank you to the people whose work made yours possible.

Circle the five reporting verbs in this article.
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs A–C, Group B on D–E, Group C on F–G. Read your part, agree on its main idea, then form new mixed groups and teach it in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Who deserves more credit: the person with the first idea, or the person who makes it work for everyone? Use one idea from the article.

Language toolkit: reporting verbs

10 MIN

Reporting verbs tell the reader who said something — and how they said it.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the article and complete them.

1. (B) Bell received the patent, but some historians that others reached similar ideas …

2. (B) His team’s real achievement, as historians often , was to make the bulb practical …

3. (D) Supporters that this system is fair …

4. (E) Teachers , however, that software can only find copied words …

5. (G) The history of invention a simple lesson.

Five verbs, five jobs rule
VerbUse it when the writer …Example
arguesgives reasons for an opinionKarimova (2021) argues that inventions are teamwork.
claimssays something is true (you may not agree)Some companies claim that their software finds all copying.
explainsmakes how or why clearRakhimov (2019) explains how a paraphrase is built.
suggestsgives an idea politely, not stronglyRakhimov (2019) suggests that teachers show examples.
points outdraws attention to an important factKarimova (2021) points out that many inventors are forgotten.

Direct speech = quotation

Karimova writes, “An invention is rarely a single flash of genius” (2021, p. 14).
→ exact words · quotation marks · page number

Reported speech = paraphrase

Karimova (2021) argues that an invention is rarely the result of one sudden idea.
→ verb + that · no quotation marks · your words

  • she / he + verb-s: Karimova argue ✗ → Karimova argues ✓ (present simple is normal in academic writing)
  • explain / suggest: explains me that ✗ → explains (to us) that ✓ · suggests to check ✗ → suggests checking ✓
  • Change the person: “I believe …” → Karimova (2021) says that she believes …
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. Rakhimov argue that students copy out of fear.
2. Karimova explains us that ideas grow slowly.
3. According to Karimova, she says that patents are useful.
4. The author suggests to check every source.
5. Karimova claims “that inventions are teamwork.”

Karimova (2021) and Rakhimov (2019) are fictional authors made for this lesson. You will meet their books in step 5.

Level up: report with precision

CONTINUED

At C1 your reporting verb does two jobs: it tells the reader what the author does (argues, admits, doubts) and what you think of it. A summary also becomes shorter and denser with nouns.

ToolPhrasesExample
Precise reporting verbs
what the author does		contends · maintains · acknowledges · questions · notesKarimova (2021) contends that inventions are rarely the work of one person.
Hedged reporting
a careful claim		suggests that … may · appears to · it would seem thatRakhimov (2019) suggests that fear may push students to copy.
Nominalisation
verb → noun in summaries		argue → argument · explain → explanation · achieve → achievementKarimova’s argument that inventions are teamwork is convincing.
Your stance on the source
evaluate it		rightly · convincingly · overlooks · is persuasiveRakhimov rightly points out that … · This view overlooks …

Task: Who deserves the credit for an invention? Write a paragraph. Use Source A.
Topic sentence
The person whose name is on an invention is rarely the only person who deserves the credit.
Paraphrase
As Karimova (2021) explains, most inventions grow slowly from the small steps of many different people.
Quotation
In her words, an invention is “usually the last step on a long staircase built by many hands” (Karimova, 2021, p. 14).
Your voice
The telephone is a good example: several inventors were working on similar devices in the 1870s, but most people today remember only one name. In my view, the famous inventor still deserves credit for making the idea work, but textbooks should mention the others too.
Concluding
In short, the credit for an invention should be shared, just as the work was.
Reference
Karimova, D. (2021). Small sparks: How inventions really happen. Caravan Books.

Make the mark: cite your sources

CONTINUED

Every borrowed tile needs its mark in two places: a short mark in your text and a full mark in the reference list at the end. This book uses a simple version of APA style.

1 · In your text: (Author, year)

  • Name first: Karimova (2021) argues that …
  • Name at the end: … many hands (Karimova, 2021).
  • Quotation: “…” (Karimova, 2021, p. 14).
  • Family name only — no first name, no initial.

2 · At the end: the reference list

Karimova, D.(2021).Small sparks: How inventions really happen.Caravan Books.

Family name, initial. · (Year). · Title in italics — capital letter only for the first word and after a colon. · Publisher.

Write the reference line for Source B. Use the details on the source card.

☆Correct the marks.

Wrong markCorrect mark
1. … built by many hands (Dilnoza Karimova, 2021).
2. … built by many hands (2021, Karimova).
3. “A paraphrase is not a disguise” (Rakhimov).
Honest or stolen? judge

Original (Karimova, 2021, p. 27): “Many inventors are remembered not because they had an idea first, but because they made it work for ordinary people.”

Student’s sentenceHonestStolen
1. Many inventors are remembered not because they had an idea first, but because they made it work for ordinary people.
2. “Many inventors are remembered not because they had an idea first, but because they made it work for ordinary people” (Karimova, 2021, p. 27).
3. Inventors often become famous because they made an idea useful for everyone, not because they thought of it first.
4. Karimova (2021) points out that inventors often become famous because they made an idea useful for everyone, not because they thought of it first.
5. Many inventors are remembered not since they had a thought first, but since they made it function for normal people (Karimova, 2021).

The paraphrase recipe

1 Read until you understand.  2 Hide the original.  3 Write the idea from memory, in a new sentence structure.  4 Check: no four words in a row copied (key terms such as invention are fine).  5 Add the mark: (Author, year).

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own paragraph.

CriterionA C1 paragraph …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear main idea from the topic sentence to the concluding sentence
O · Organisationmoves from topic sentence → source (paraphrase, quotation) → your voice → concluding sentence, marks every source, and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: reporting verbs (argues / points out that …, he / she + -s) and quotation marks

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students answered the Level 2 task (Why do some students plagiarise?) with Source B. Mark both.

Student A
Many students are copying because they are afraid, not because they are lazy. Rakhimov say that Students often copy not because they are lazy, but because they are afraid that their own words are not good enough (2019). I am agree with him. For example, my friend copied an essay because her English was weak. University must punish the students, but it must also teach paraphrase. In my opinion I think plagiat is very bad thing.
Student B
Plagiarism is often seen as a sign of laziness, yet its causes may be more complex. Rakhimov (2019) contends that many students copy out of fear that their own English is not good enough. If this is the case, punishment alone is unlikely to solve the problem. As he puts it, a paraphrase is “proof that you have understood” (Rakhimov, 2019, p. 41); universities would therefore do better to teach paraphrasing as a skill.

1. Many students are copying because … →

2. Rakhimov say that Students often copy … →

3. I am agree with him. →

4. University must punish the students. →

5. In my opinion I think … →

6. plagiat is very bad thing →

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

A

Part A · Reading

22 MIN · 10 POINTS

Warm-up (not scored): how many minutes does it take you to walk from home to the nearest shop? Now read the article and answer questions 1–10 in the next section.

Ten Minutes from Home

A magazine article · about 360 words · B2+ · written for this book

AImagine an ordinary weekday. You wake up, walk five minutes to the bakery for warm bread, take your little brother to the school around the corner and then meet your friends in a small park. You do not need a car, a taxi or even a bus. For many families in Uzbekistan, this is not a dream. It is simply life in a mahalla.

BAround the world, city planners are now discussing a similar idea. They call it the “15-minute city”: a city where people can reach most of the places they need every day — shops, schools, clinics, parks and even their workplaces — in a short walk or bike ride from home. Supporters believe that such neighbourhoods are healthier, cleaner and friendlier.

CThe reasons are easy to understand. When people walk instead of driving, they move more and breathe cleaner air. Streets with fewer cars are quieter and safer for children. Local shops benefit too, because people buy their bread, fruit and medicine close to home rather than in a distant shopping centre.

DHowever, the idea is not perfect. Critics point out that not every job can move close to people’s homes. A factory, a university or a large hospital needs a lot of space, and many people will always travel to reach one. Others worry that strict planning rules may limit people’s freedom to drive where they want.

ECities in Uzbekistan face their own version of this question. From Tashkent to Jizzakh, cities are growing, and new apartment districts are appearing on their edges. Some of these districts have wide roads and tall buildings, but few shops, trees or places to sit. Residents often have to travel to the old centre for almost everything. In the morning the roads into the centre are full, while the new districts stay quiet and empty.

FPerhaps part of the answer lies in an old tradition. A good mahalla has always had a teahouse, a small market, a school and a guzar where neighbours meet and talk. If new districts learned from it, the cities of the future might feel a little more like the neighbourhoods of the past.

Read once for the main ideas, then again for the questions.

Word help. city planner — a person who decides how a city grows · critic — a person who says what is wrong with an idea · version — one form of something · strict — firm, with no exceptions · guzar — the square or meeting place of a mahalla

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Practise them on two paragraphs first, then use them on your own paragraph.

CriterionA C1 paragraph …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear idea from the topic sentence to the concluding sentence
O · Organisationhas one idea per paragraph (topic sentence · support · concluding sentence) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: the grammar of Module 1 (present tenses, there is / are, adjective order, reporting verbs)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students wrote Task 1 (Describe one place in your city that you love). Mark both.

Student A
My favourite place in my city is the park near the river. It is very nice and very beautiful. There are many old trees, a small lake and many peoples. Every weekend I am playing football there with my friends, and in the evening families walk along the river. Also there is a café with cheap tea. In conclusion, I love this park because it is nice.
Student B
Few places capture the spirit of my city as vividly as the old public library in the centre. From early morning, its quiet reading rooms fill with students preparing for exams, while retired teachers read the newspapers by the tall arched windows. In the courtyard, young parents read picture books to their children under an ancient plane tree. Arguably, the library is less a store of books than a meeting place — without it, the city would lose much of its heart.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Level up: from a B2 to a C1 paragraph

15 MIN

Your foundation is laid. These four tools turn a correct paragraph into a C1 one: you report sources precisely, point back instead of repeating, pack actions into nouns and make claims carefully.

ToolPhrasesExample
Reporting verbs
stone 5: use sources		suggests · argues · points out · claimsThe writer suggests that new districts could learn from the mahalla.
Reference words
stone 4: link ideas		this / such + noun · these districts · this ideaSuch neighbourhoods are healthier and friendlier.
Nominalisation
verb or adjective → noun		grow → growth · plan → planning · free → freedomCities grow fast. → The rapid growth of cities puts pressure on roads.
Hedging
a careful claim		tend to · may · it would appear that · arguablyResidents of new districts tend to drive to the centre.
Notice find it

Find four phrases in the Part A article that report other people’s views or make a claim less certain. Write the paragraph letter.

1. ( )

2. ( )

3. ( )

4. ( )

Make it C1 rewrite

Rewrite each sentence with the word(s) in brackets. Keep the meaning.

B2 sentenceC1 sentence
1. People in new districts usually drive to the centre. (tend to)
2. The article says that streets with fewer cars are safer. (points out)
3. Cities are growing very fast. This puts pressure on roads. (The rapid growth)
4. Some districts have no shops. Districts like these feel empty. (Such)
5. New districts are worse than the old centre. (arguably … less lively)

Remember from Stop 1: do not over-hedge

✗ It might perhaps be possible that a 15-minute city could maybe be a little healthier.
✓ A 15-minute city is arguably healthier.  — one hedge per claim is enough.

Level up: words and phrases

CONTINUED

Level up · C1 words: walkable (easy and pleasant to walk around) · urban sprawl (the uncontrolled spread of a city into the land around it) · infrastructure (the roads, pipes and services a city needs) · liveable (pleasant and suitable to live in)

Word families: plan → planner → planning · reside → resident → residential · walk → walkable → walkability · pedestrian → pedestrianise → pedestrianisation

JobB2 · safeC1 · upgrade

Common traps

✗ In my city there is many parks.
✓ In my city there are many parks.
✗ The people in my mahalla is very friendly.
✓ The people in my mahalla are very friendly.
✗ I am living in Jizzakh since 2015.
✓ I have lived in Jizzakh since 2015.
✗ It is an old wooden small teahouse.
✓ It is a small old wooden teahouse.
✗ According to the writer says that parks are important.
✓ According to the writer, parks are important.
✗ My favourite place is park.
✓ My favourite place is the park.
✗ The traffic is very much in the morning.
✓ The traffic is very heavy in the morning.
✗ The infrastructure of our district are old.
✓ The infrastructure of our district is old.
Use one C1 phrase per part of the paragraph, not five in one sentence.
